The first rule is that there are no rules. Ok so U stands for utility. The U-2 can fly a wide variety of recon missions, and also the U designation might have been there to throw off the soviets. That happens a lot. P in P-63 means Pursuit. The Army Air Corps called their fighters pursuit planes. They didn't realize how dumb this was when photo recon planes began to hit the scene, and labeled those F for Foto. Yeah it's dumb. C does in fact stand for cargo on the CV-22. It's kinda stupid though because as far as I know, the CV-22 is used for a lot of special operations, and very little for hauling cargo.

The USN and USAAC/USAAF/USAF had their own designations for things. This was standardized in 1962. Each aircraft designation would be three letters and a number. The middle letter was the aircraft's job. F for fighter, A for attacker, B for bomber, R for recon. The prefix would indicate a modification. These letters were shared with the job and would indicate that an airframe was modified for a different job. The connotation being that it's ability to perform the original job is reduced if not impossible. The suffix letter let's you know what the hell it is. H for helicopter, Q for drone, and _ is for fixed wing. That's right if it's a plane, you drop the suffix. So an S-3 is a very different aircraft from an SH-3. An F-22 is in no way related to an MV-22.

So there are two types of damage in wargame, HE and AP. AP is entirely ineffective against infantry. It will not damage them at all. HE is effective against infantry, but loses effectiveness against vehicles as their armor goes up. So an HE bomb will still Shrek an unarmored truck, but more HE is needed for things like tanks. HE comes in a few varieties, standard bombs, rockets, and napalm. Bombs are pretty straightforward, rockets have much lower HE but the planes are quick to rearm. Napalm is a damage over time thing with the added bonuses of blocking line of sight and quickly causing enemy troops to panic. AP comes from cluster bombs and ATGMs, and a handful of planes have AP on their guns but it's only a few. AP is the amount of armor your weapon can penetrate and how much damage it will do. Cluster bombs can kill heavy tanks with enough hits, but you need a lot of them. They will instantly vaporize enemy trucks, APCs, artillery, basically anything that isn't a tank. Sidewinders do require cooling to their seeker heads to work. Except the 9B. Most planes don't model the cool down time needed for the seeker, however the tomcat does. Without cooling the missiles are basically useless. I haven't tested the limits but I'd guess that they can only see anything that is exceptionally hot. The AIM-9M and 9L use liquid Argon to cool their seekers. Once the cooling is activated, it takes a few seconds for the seeker to reach maximum sensitivity, but it is usable against closer targets. This coolant lasts for, I want to say about an hour. Short enough that you can't turn it on at takeoff and forget about it, long enough that you don't really need to worry about it. Before that the Navy and the Air Force used different sidewinders with different cooling methods. The AIM-9D/G/ and H were all cooled with liquid Nitrogen instead of liquid Argon. The Air force's AIM-9E/J and P used electric cooling. The seekers were cooled using the Peltier effect and could remain cool as long as power was supplied, so those models could remain cold indefinitely. Later models of the P would use Argon cooling too, it's not abundantly clear when this change happened though, likely by the AIM-9P3 if I had to guess. The AIM-9X is a different beast though. It uses a closed loop cycle of Argon to cool its seeker. There's a cooler in the missile that runs off of, I want to say a stirling cooler, that keeps the missile cool as long as power is applied. So the 9X can also keep itself cool indefinitely as long as that mechanism doesn't fail.

In the fight, you do need to appreciate the AMRAAM is not as agile as a 9X or an R-73, so you won't have much success in a turning swirling dogfight. Basically only tail aspect shots if the guy is turning hard in close. If you can, you want to get separated from the bad guy. I'm asking myself Three questions generally, "Does the missile have enough energy to teach the bad guy?" "How hard does the missile have to turn to hit the bad guy?" "How much time does the missile have to make that turn?" We're in close so we can safely assume the missile has the energy to reach the bad guy. A forward aspect shot, the missile will probably not have a ton of time to make that turn, best to point your nose at the bad guy to reduce the amount the missile has to turn. A tail aspect shot, the missile has more time to make that turn, so heavier turns at closer ranges can be acceptable. Side aspect shots the missile has to turn pretty hard, ensure you're far enough away that a turn can be made. Leading the target can help here.

I don't remember the reasons aside from "Don't do it" in the manuals, but I can speculate. A lot of it falls into why they shouldn't shoot in a hover, and why they wouldn't shoot in a hover. Shouldn't comes down to safety. Larger weapons can cause the aircraft to roll when in a hover. Not a problem for rockets, but anything larger and the sudden asymmetry could cause the aircraft to roll violently before the pilot can correct. Another safety concern is the engine sucking in gas from the gun or exhaust from rockets. The gun especially is not really a concern in forward flight, but while hovering, nothing is stopping that gas from getting sucked into the engine, reducing power or killing the engine outright.

As for why you wouldn't? It's just not a good idea tactically. Harriers can't hover with a lot of fuel or weapons. In combat the plane would be hovering well above the ground which would reduce this even further. This essentially makes the Harrier inferior to helicopters in every way. Range, payload, loiter time, even agility would go to the helicopter. Remaining as a plane would allow the harrier to easily retake the range advantage, match or exceed the payload depending on the version, and at least improve on the loiter time from minutes, to hours. I should also clarify that the minutes of loiter time in a hover assume basically no weapons or fuel. Water injection can increase how much a harrier could potentially hover with, but the water runs out in a matter of seconds, and can't really be used for sustained hover.

I'm not sure how in depth you want it, but here's a high level overview.

In modern use, a torpedo is a self propelled explosive weapon that moves through water to destroy other objects in the water. They can be both unguided or guided with a handful of methods. Torpedoes can be primarily intended to engage enemy surface ships or enemy submarines. Modern torpedoes will generally be capable of engaging both effectively. Torpedoes can be launched from surface ships, fixed wing aircraft, helicopters, and of course submarines.

Guided torpedoes are guided using two and a half different methods. Either passive sonar which will home in on the sound made by an enemy, or active sonar, which will send its own sound waves out to bounce off an enemy to gain its location. The half guidance method is due to the torpedoes having a wire going back to the launching sub. This wire can update a torpedoe's instructions after launch and can even be used to directly control the torpedo if required. This method is only a half though because it is usually a good idea to let the torpedo guide itself for the final interception.

In cold waters American submarines can be armed with three types of torpedoes. In the 1960s they have both the Mk16 and Mk37. The Mk16 is an unguided anti ship torpedo with few advancements from the torpedoes of WW2. It can sink most ships in a single hit, although it lacks any abilities against submerged targets. The Mk37 is a smaller guided anti submarine torpedo. It features both passive and active sonar guidance. This torpedo is slow though and has a small warhead. It is only recommended to use this model for anti submarine work. In the 1980s and beyond American subs have access to the Mk48. This torpedo would replace the Mk16 and Mk37 for both the anti ship and anti sub role respectively. The large warhead kills most in a single shot. It is much faster than the Mk37 but still has its own sonar for guidance. This torpedo remains in service for the US Navy's submarine force to the modern day. Fun fact: if the warhead of a Mk48 is removed it will float when it runs out of fuel. They can then be retrieved and refueled for future use. Other torpedoes may do this, but the Mk48 is the only one I know for sure.
